title: Emily Roebling Finishes the Brooklyn Bridge
text:
John Augustus Roebling designed the Brooklyn Bridge, but he never saw it begun. In 1869, while surveying the site, his foot was crushed by a ferry against a piling, and he died of tetanus weeks later. His son Washington, an engineer and Civil War veteran, took over as chief engineer.

Washington worked inside the caissons, the huge pressurized chambers sunk to the river bottom for the foundations. In 1872 he was struck down by caisson disease, the bends. Partly paralyzed and in great pain, he could not visit the site. From a room in Brooklyn Heights he watched the work through a telescope.

His wife, Emily Warren Roebling, became his link to the project. She carried his instructions to the engineers, answered their questions, and dealt with officials and contractors. To do it, she studied stress analysis, cable construction and the strength of materials. For about eleven years she was so present on the project that many people believed she was the real engineer. When politicians tried to remove her husband in 1882, she defended him before the American Society of Civil Engineers.

The bridge opened on 24 May 1883. Emily Roebling was the first person to cross it by carriage, carrying a rooster as a sign of victory. A plaque on the bridge honors the three of them: John, Washington and Emily.
lesson: When illness strikes a family, the work does not have to die. Someone willing to learn what was never expected of her can carry it through.
people: Emily Warren Roebling, Washington Roebling, John A. Roebling
location: Brooklyn and New York City, USA
source: David McCullough, The Great Bridge (1972); Roebling family papers, Rutgers University
